sn42.9:1.1.pli: Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ yena nāḷandā tadavasari.
sn42.9:1.1.eng: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at Nāḷandā.
sn42.9:1.1.comm: There seems to be some confusion in the location, as Nāḷandā is in Magadha, not Kosala. See notes below and another possible confusion at SN 42.11:1.1.

sn42.9:1.2.pli: Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā nāḷandāyaṃ viharati pāvārikambavane.
sn42.9:1.2.eng: There he stayed near Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s mango grove.

sn42.9:2.1.pli: Tena kho pana samayena nāḷandā dubbhikkhā hoti dvīhitikā setaṭṭhikā salākāvuttā.
sn42.9:2.1.eng: Now at that time Nāḷandā was undergoing famine and scarcity, with crops blighted and turned to straw.
sn42.9:2.1.comm: Read duhitikā setaṭṭikā as proposed by von Hinüber (“The Ghost Word Dvı̄hitikā and the Description of Famines in Early Buddhist Literature”) and adopted by Bodhi (Connected Discourses, note on this passage).

sn42.9:2.2.pli: Tena kho pana samayena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto nāḷandāyaṃ paṭivasati mahatiyā nigaṇṭhaparisāya saddhiṃ.
sn42.9:2.2.eng: At that time the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan was residing at Nāḷandā together with a large assembly of Jain ascetics.
sn42.9:2.2.comm: Jain tradition holds that Mahāvīra passed at a Pāvā near Nāḷandā. Buddhist texts know only the Pāvā of the Mallians to the north. Evidently there has been some confusion, and perhaps “Pāvārika’s mango grove”, the site of discussions with Jains here and at MN 56, is the Pāvā known to the Jains. Note, however, that the earliest Jain source for Mahāvīra’s passing, the Kalpasutra, does not say where Pāvā is. But it does say the events were commemorated by the rulers of Kāsī and Kosala, and the Mallians and the Licchavīs. The absence of Magadha and the presence of Malla sit better with the location of Pāvā in Malla rather than Magadha. Malla bordered Kosala and may have been considered under its sway (as was Sakya).

sn42.9:2.3.pli: Atha kho asibandhakaputto gāmaṇi nigaṇṭhasāvako yena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā nigaṇṭhaṃ nāṭaputtaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho asibandhakaputtaṃ gāmaṇiṃ nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto etadavoca:
sn42.9:2.3.eng: Then Asibandhaka’s son the chief, who was a disciple of the Jains, went up to the Jain Ñātika, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Jain Ñātika said to him:

sn42.9:2.4.pli: “ehi tvaṃ, gāmaṇi, samaṇassa gotamassa vādaṃ āropehi.
sn42.9:2.4.eng: “Come, chief, refute the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine.

sn42.9:2.5.eng: Then you will get a good reputation:

sn42.9:2.6.pli: ‘asibandhakaputtena gāmaṇinā samaṇassa gotamassa evaṃmahiddhikassa evaṃmahānubhāvassa vādo āropito’”ti.
sn42.9:2.6.eng: ‘Asibandhaka’s son the chief refuted the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama, so mighty and powerful!’”

sn42.9:3.1.pli: “Kathaṃ panāhaṃ, bhante, samaṇassa gotamassa evaṃmahiddhikassa evaṃmahānubhāvassa vādaṃ āropessāmī”ti?
sn42.9:3.1.eng: “But sir, how am I to do this?”

sn42.9:3.2.pli: “Ehi tvaṃ, gāmaṇi, yena samaṇo gotamo tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ evaṃ vadehi:
sn42.9:3.2.eng: “Here, brahmin, go to the ascetic Gotama and say to him:

sn42.9:3.3.pli: ‘nanu, bhante, bhagavā anekapariyāyena kulānaṃ anuddayaṃ vaṇṇeti, anurakkhaṃ vaṇṇeti, anukampaṃ vaṇṇetī’ti?
sn42.9:3.3.eng: ‘Sir, don’t you in many ways praise kindness, protection, and sympathy for families?’

sn42.9:3.4.pli: Sace kho, gāmaṇi, samaṇo gotamo evaṃ puṭṭho evaṃ byākaroti:
sn42.9:3.4.eng: When he’s asked this, if he answers:

sn42.9:3.5.pli: ‘evaṃ, gāmaṇi, tathāgato anekapariyāyena kulānaṃ anuddayaṃ vaṇṇeti, anurakkhaṃ vaṇṇeti, anukampaṃ vaṇṇetī’ti, tamenaṃ tvaṃ evaṃ vadeyyāsi:
sn42.9:3.5.eng: ‘Indeed I do, chief,’ say this to him:

sn42.9:3.6.pli: ‘atha kiñcarahi, bhante, bhagavā dubbhikkhe dvīhitike setaṭṭhike salākāvutte mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ cārikaṃ carati?
sn42.9:3.6.eng: ‘So what then are you doing, wandering together with this large Saṅgha of mendicants during a time of famine and scarcity, with crops blighted and turned to straw?
sn42.9:3.6.comm: Cf. Mahākassapa’s criticism of Ānanda at SN 16.11.

sn42.9:3.7.pli: Ucchedāya bhagavā kulānaṃ paṭipanno, anayāya bhagavā kulānaṃ paṭipanno, upaghātāya bhagavā kulānaṃ paṭipanno’ti.
sn42.9:3.7.eng: The Buddha is practicing to annihilate, collapse, and ruin families!’
sn42.9:3.7.comm: Renunciates, relying on alms offered by the lay community, were careful to not put them under undue pressure. This is discussed often in the Vinaya, for example the introduction to Bu Ss 6.

sn42.9:3.8.pli: Imaṃ kho te, gāmaṇi, samaṇo gotamo ubhatokoṭikaṃ pañhaṃ puṭṭho neva sakkhati uggilituṃ, neva sakkhati ogilitun”ti.
sn42.9:3.8.eng: When you put this dilemma to him, the Buddha won’t be able to either spit it out or swallow it down.”

sn42.9:3.9.pli: “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho asibandhakaputto gāmaṇi nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa paṭissutvā uṭṭhāyāsanā nigaṇṭhaṃ nāṭaputtaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho asibandhakaputto gāmaṇi bhagavantaṃ etadavoca:
sn42.9:3.9.eng: “Yes, sir,” replied Asibandhaka’s son. He got up from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Jain Ñātika, keeping him on his right. Then he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

sn42.9:4.1.pli: “Nanu, bhante, bhagavā anekapariyāyena kulānaṃ anuddayaṃ vaṇṇeti, anurakkhaṃ vaṇṇeti, anukampaṃ vaṇṇetī”ti?
sn42.9:4.1.eng: “Sir, don’t you in many ways praise kindness, protection, and sympathy for families?”

sn42.9:4.2.pli: “Evaṃ, gāmaṇi, tathāgato anekapariyāyena kulānaṃ anuddayaṃ vaṇṇeti, anurakkhaṃ vaṇṇeti, anukampaṃ vaṇṇetī”ti.

sn42.9:4.3.pli: “Atha kiñcarahi, bhante, bhagavā dubbhikkhe dvīhitike setaṭṭhike salākāvutte mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ cārikaṃ carati?
sn42.9:4.3.eng: “So what then are you doing, wandering together with this large Saṅgha of mendicants during a time of famine and scarcity, with crops blighted and turned to straw?

sn42.9:4.4.pli: Ucchedāya bhagavā kulānaṃ paṭipanno, anayāya bhagavā kulānaṃ paṭipanno, upaghātāya bhagavā kulānaṃ paṭipanno”ti.
sn42.9:4.4.eng: The Buddha is practicing to annihilate, collapse, and ruin families!”

sn42.9:4.5.pli: “Ito so, gāmaṇi, ekanavutikappe yamahaṃ anussarāmi, nābhijānāmi kiñci kulaṃ pakkabhikkhānuppadānamattena upahatapubbaṃ.
sn42.9:4.5.eng: “Well, chief, I recollect ninety-one eons back but I’m not aware of any family that’s been ruined merely by offering some cooked almsfood.
sn42.9:4.5.comm: This is the time of the Buddha Vipassī (DN 14:1.4.1).

sn42.9:4.6.pli: Atha kho yāni tāni kulāni aḍḍhāni mahaddhanāni mahābhogāni pahūtajātarūparajatāni pahūtavittūpakaraṇāni pahūtadhanadhaññāni, sabbāni tāni dānasambhūtāni ceva saccasambhūtāni ca sāmaññasambhūtāni ca.
sn42.9:4.6.eng: Rather, rich, affluent, and wealthy families—with lots of gold and silver, lots of property and assets, and lots of money and grain—all acquired their wealth because of giving, truth, and restraint.
sn42.9:4.6.comm: Read saññama (“restraint”) per BJT and PTS rather than MS sāmañña (“equality”). Compare the stock list, “giving, self-control, restraint, and truthfulness” (SN 42.13:18.6).

sn42.9:4.7.pli: Aṭṭha kho, gāmaṇi, hetū, aṭṭha paccayā kulānaṃ upaghātāya.
sn42.9:4.7.eng: Chief, there are eight causes and reasons for the ruin of families.

sn42.9:4.8.pli: Rājato vā kulāni upaghātaṃ gacchanti, corato vā kulāni upaghātaṃ gacchanti, aggito vā kulāni upaghātaṃ gacchanti, udakato vā kulāni upaghātaṃ gacchanti, nihitaṃ vā ṭhānā vigacchati, duppayuttā vā kammantā vipajjanti, kule vā kulaṅgāroti uppajjati, yo te bhoge vikirati vidhamati viddhaṃseti, aniccatāyeva aṭṭhamīti.
sn42.9:4.8.eng: Their ruin stems from rulers, bandits, fire, or flood. Or they lose their savings. Or their business fails due to not applying themselves to work. Or a wastrel is born into the family who squanders and fritters away their wealth. And impermanence is the eighth.
sn42.9:4.8.comm: This passage is unique, but see SN 3.19:3.3, MN 14:9.3, AN 8.54:3.4. | Follow MS reading nihitaṁ vā ṭhānā vigacchati, “what is laid down disappears from its place” i.e. they lose their savings. BJT and PTS have nihitaṁ vā nādhigacchati, “does not find their savings”. Compare Kp 8:4.1, nidhi vā ṭhānā cavati, “savings shift from their place”.

sn42.9:4.9.pli: Ime kho, gāmaṇi, aṭṭha hetū, aṭṭha paccayā kulānaṃ upaghātāya.
sn42.9:4.9.eng: These are the eight causes and reasons for the ruin of families.

sn42.9:4.10.pli: Imesu kho, gāmaṇi, aṭṭhasu hetūsu, aṭṭhasu paccayesu saṃvijjamānesu yo maṃ evaṃ vadeyya:
sn42.9:4.10.eng: Given that these eight reasons are found, suppose someone says this:

sn42.9:4.11.pli: ‘ucchedāya bhagavā kulānaṃ paṭipanno, anayāya bhagavā kulānaṃ paṭipanno, upaghātāya bhagavā kulānaṃ paṭipanno’ti,
sn42.9:4.11.eng: ‘The Buddha is practicing to annihilate, collapse, and ruin families!’

sn42.9:4.12.pli: taṃ, gāmaṇi, vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye”ti.
sn42.9:4.12.eng: Unless they give up that speech and that thought, and let go of that view, they will be placed in hell as if delivered there.”

sn42.9:5.1.pli: Evaṃ vutte, asibandhakaputto gāmaṇi bhagavantaṃ etadavoca:
sn42.9:5.1.eng: When he said this, Asibandhaka’s son the chief said to the Buddha,

sn42.9:5.3.pli: upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gatan”ti.
sn42.9:5.3.eng: From this day forth, may the Buddha remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

sn43.1:1.2.eng: “Mendicants, I will teach you the unconditioned and the path that leads to the unconditioned.
sn43.1:1.2.comm: In Vedic usage, something that is saṅkhata (Sanskrit saṁskṛta, “conditioned”) has been worked through a process (saṅkhāra) that shapes it into its “completed” or “perfected” form (eg. Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 7.1.2.6). To be saṅkhata is to be “equipped” for battle (Rig Veda 8.33.9) or “prepared” for the ritual (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 8.6.1.1). When natural language is “refined” through meticulous grammar, it becomes saṅkhata, or as we say today, “Sanskrit”. Linguistically, it is a past participle, describing something that has been made into this form. But it also conveys the sense of something “readied” or “energized” or “charged” and thus fit for purpose, “potent” to perform its function. The Buddha inverts the Vedic value system, positioning the “unconditioned” Nibbāna as independent of Vedic or other rituals of “potentization”. Asaṅkhata conveys the sense of “unworked” (as a natural gem), or “unconsecrated” (by Vedic rites) and thus implies a raw or natural state. In Pali, asaṅkhata is used as an adjective describing something; but that something is unstated as the referent is empty. So whereas in English we say, “the unconditioned”, in Pali it is just “unconditioned” and does not imply an existent state or reality that is unconditioned. The prefix saṁ is sometimes said to mean “together” yielding the sense “compounded”, but usage suggests the primary sense of saṁ here is “good, well, perfect”. Nor does saṅkhata convey the sense “created” or “fabricated”, but rather “processed”. This aligns with the Buddhist rejection of creation from nothing. Existence is an ongoing process, inheriting what was made in the past, processing and potentizing it and thereby shaping the future. The English word “conditioned” conveys these senses quite well, implying something dependent on conditions, shaped into a specified state, or prepared for a given purpose.

sn43.1:1.5.eng: The ending of greed, hate, and delusion.
sn43.1:1.5.comm: The unconditioned is not “produced” by the eightfold path, but rather, the practice of the path leads to the cessation of greed, hate, and delusion, which are the conditions for suffering. This series of discourses all make the same point, each highlighting a particular way of describing the path.

sn43.1:1.7.eng: And what is the path that leads to the unconditioned?

sn43.1:1.8.comm: Treated in detail in the Kāyagatāsatisutta (MN 119).

sn43.1:1.9.eng: This is called the path that leads to the unconditioned.

sn43.1:2.1.pli: Iti kho, bhikkhave, desitaṃ vo mayā asaṅkhataṃ, desito asaṅkhatagāmimaggo.
sn43.1:2.1.eng: So, mendicants, I’ve taught you the unconditioned and the path that leads to the unconditioned.

sn43.1:2.2.pli: Yaṃ, bhikkhave, satthārā karaṇīyaṃ sāvakānaṃ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṃ upādāya, kataṃ vo taṃ mayā.
sn43.1:2.2.eng: Out of sympathy, I’ve done what a teacher should do who wants what’s best for their disciples.

sn43.1:2.3.pli: Etāni, bhikkhave, rukkhamūlāni, etāni suññāgārāni. Jhāyatha, bhikkhave, mā pamādattha; mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī”ti.
sn43.1:2.3.eng: Here are these roots of trees, and here are these empty huts. Practice absorption, mendicants! Don’t be negligent! Don’t regret it later! This is my instruction to you.”

sn43.10:1.1.eng: “And what is the path that leads to the unconditioned?

sn43.10:1.2.pli: Satta bojjhaṅgā. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo …pe….

sn43.11:1.1.eng: “And what is the path that leads to the unconditioned?

sn43.11:1.3.eng: This is called the path that leads to the unconditioned.

sn43.11:1.4.eng: So, mendicants, I’ve taught you the unconditioned and the path that leads to the unconditioned.

sn43.11:1.5.pli: Yaṃ, bhikkhave, satthārā karaṇīyaṃ sāvakānaṃ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṃ upādāya kataṃ vo taṃ mayā.
sn43.11:1.5.eng: Out of sympathy, I’ve done what a teacher should do who wants what’s best for their disciples.

sn43.11:1.6.pli: Etāni, bhikkhave, rukkhamūlāni, etāni suññāgārāni. Jhāyatha, bhikkhave, mā pamādattha; mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī”ti.
sn43.11:1.6.eng: Here are these roots of trees, and here are these empty huts. Practice absorption, mendicants! Don’t be negligent! Don’t regret it later! This is my instruction to you.”

sn43.12:1.1.eng: “Mendicants, I will teach you the unconditioned and the path that leads to the unconditioned.
sn43.12:1.1.comm: This discourse repeats and sometimes expands the previous chapter.

sn43.12:1.4.eng: The ending of greed, hate, and delusion.

sn43.12:1.6.eng: And what is the path that leads to the unconditioned?

sn43.12:1.8.eng: This is called the path that leads to the unconditioned.

sn43.12:1.9.pli: Iti kho, bhikkhave, desitaṃ vo mayā asaṅkhataṃ, desito asaṅkhatagāmimaggo.
sn43.12:1.9.eng: So, mendicants, I’ve taught you the unconditioned and the path that leads to the unconditioned.

sn43.12:1.10.pli: Yaṃ, bhikkhave, satthārā karaṇīyaṃ sāvakānaṃ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṃ upādāya, kataṃ vo taṃ mayā.
sn43.12:1.10.eng: Out of sympathy, I’ve done what a teacher should do who wants what’s best for their disciples.

sn43.12:1.11.pli: Etāni, bhikkhave, rukkhamūlāni, etāni suññāgārāni. Jhāyatha, bhikkhave, mā pamādattha; mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanīti.
sn43.12:1.11.eng: Here are these roots of trees, and here are these empty huts. Practice absorption, mendicants! Don’t be negligent! Don’t regret it later! This is my instruction to you.”

sn43.12:2.1.pli: Asaṅkhatañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi asaṅkhatagāmiñca maggaṃ.
sn43.12:2.1.eng: “Mendicants, I will teach you the unconditioned and the path that leads to the unconditioned.

sn43.12:2.4.eng: The ending of greed, hate, and delusion.

sn43.12:2.6.eng: And what is the path that leads to the unconditioned?

sn43.12:2.8.eng: This is called the path that leads to the unconditioned. …”

sn43.12:2.9.pli: Iti kho, bhikkhave, desitaṃ vo mayā asaṅkhataṃ …pe…

sn43.12:3.1.eng: “And what is the path that leads to the unconditioned?

sn43.12:3.2.eng: Immersion with placing the mind and keeping it connected. …

sn43.12:3.5.eng: Immersion without placing the mind, merely keeping it connected. …

sn43.12:3.8.pli: Avitakko avicāro samādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo …pe….
sn43.12:3.8.eng: Immersion without placing the mind or keeping it connected. …

sn43.12:4.8.pli: Appaṇihito samādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo …pe….

sn43.12:5.2.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.
sn43.12:5.2.eng: A mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. …

sn43.12:5.5.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati …pe…
sn43.12:5.5.eng: A mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of feelings …

sn43.12:5.8.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu citte cittānupassī viharati …pe…
sn43.12:5.8.eng: A mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the mind …

sn43.12:5.11.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati …pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo …pe….
sn43.12:5.11.eng: A mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of principles …

sn43.12:6.2.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati.
sn43.12:6.2.eng: A mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise. …

sn43.12:6.5.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati.
sn43.12:6.5.eng: A mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities are given up. …

sn43.12:6.8.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati.
sn43.12:6.8.eng: A mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that skillful qualities arise. …

sn43.12:6.11.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo …pe….
sn43.12:6.11.eng: A mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fulfilled by development. …

sn43.12:7.2.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti.
sn43.12:7.2.eng: A mendicant develops the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to enthusiasm, and active effort. …

sn43.12:7.5.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vīriyasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti.
sn43.12:7.5.eng: A mendicant develops the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to energy …

sn43.12:7.8.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cittasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti.

sn43.12:7.11.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vīmaṃsasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo …pe….
sn43.12:7.11.eng: immersion due to inquiry, and active effort. …

sn43.12:8.2.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu saddhindriyaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ.
sn43.12:8.2.eng: A mendicant develops the faculty of faith, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. …

sn43.12:8.5.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vīriyindriyaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ …pe…
sn43.12:8.5.eng: A mendicant develops the faculty of energy …

sn43.12:8.14.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paññindriyaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo …pe….
sn43.12:8.14.eng: wisdom, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. …

sn43.12:9.2.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu saddhābalaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ …pe…
sn43.12:9.2.eng: A mendicant develops the power of faith …

sn43.12:9.14.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paññābalaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo …pe….
sn43.12:9.14.eng: wisdom, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. …

sn43.12:10.2.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ …pe…
sn43.12:10.2.eng: A mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness …

sn43.12:10.10.pli: upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo …pe….
sn43.12:10.10.eng: equanimity, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. …

sn43.12:11.2.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ.

sn43.12:11.11.pli: asaṅkhatañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi asaṅkhatagāmiñca maggaṃ.

sn43.12:11.15.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sammāsamādhiṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ.
sn43.12:11.15.eng: right immersion, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go.

sn43.12:11.16.eng: This is called the path that leads to the unconditioned.

sn43.12:11.17.pli: Iti kho, bhikkhave, desitaṃ vo mayā asaṅkhataṃ, desito asaṅkhatagāmimaggo.
sn43.12:11.17.eng: So, mendicants, I’ve taught you the unconditioned and the path that leads to the unconditioned.

sn43.12:11.18.pli: Yaṃ, bhikkhave, satthārā karaṇīyaṃ sāvakānaṃ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṃ upādāya, kataṃ vo taṃ mayā.
sn43.12:11.18.eng: Out of sympathy, I’ve done what a teacher should do who wants what’s best for their disciples.

sn43.12:11.19.pli: Etāni, bhikkhave, rukkhamūlāni, etāni suññāgārāni. Jhāyatha, bhikkhave, mā pamādattha; mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī”ti.
sn43.12:11.19.eng: Here are these roots of trees, and here are these empty huts. Practice absorption, mendicants! Don’t be negligent! Don’t regret it later! This is my instruction to you.”

sn43.13:1.1.eng: “Mendicants, I will teach you the uninclined …”
sn43.13:1.1.comm: Here begins a series of synonyms for Nibbāna the unconditioned. I provide a comment for the less common term. | “Uninclined” (anata) occurs at Ud 8.2:3.1. See SN 12.40:1.4 and SN 35.87:11.5 and notes.

sn43.13:1.4.eng: (Tell in full as in the unconditioned in the previous chapter.)
